question: What is the main goal of cervical traction?

options.B: Applying a pulling force to the neck
options.D: Injecting fluid into the spinal space

explanation: You've got this! Cervical traction simply uses a steady, controlled pull on the neck to stretch the area and take off pressure. Easy peasy! [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h1)

question: How does opening up the space between spinal bones help a patient with a pinched nerve?

options.A: It permanently fuses the spinal bones together
options.B: It stops blood flow to the nerve root
options.C: It stretches the spinal cord until it snaps
options.D: It reduces pressure on the compressed nerve

explanation: Think of it like giving the nerve some breathing room! When the bones are pulled slightly apart, the squeeze is lifted, easing pain and numbness. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h1)

question: Which type of cervical traction involves putting metal pins directly into the skull bone?
explanation: Great job! Skeletal traction (like a halo device) uses metal pins right in the bone so it can handle much stronger pulling forces. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h2)

question: Why can't we use very heavy weights with skin traction?

options.A: Heavy weights will damage the skin and slip off
options.B: Skin traction requires a surgical operating room
options.C: Heavy weights make the patient fall asleep faster
options.D: Skin bones cannot support heavy metal devices

explanation: Skin is tough, but it's not made to carry heavy loads! Too much weight will cause blisters, tears, or just slip right out of the straps. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h2)

question: Which condition makes cervical traction completely unsafe (a contraindication)?
explanation: Spot on! Pulling on a broken, unstable spine can cause terrible damage to the spinal cord. Safety first! [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h3)

question: Why do patients need X-rays or scans before starting cervical traction?

options.A: To prove the patient has health insurance
options.B: To find out the patient's favorite neck position
options.C: To measure the exact weight of the patient
options.D: To check for hidden bone weakness or instability

explanation: Imaging acts like a roadmap so the healthcare team can make sure there are no surprises like hidden fractures before applying traction. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h3)

question: As a nurse, how must you make sure the traction weights are positioned during your shift?

options.A: They are adjusted upward by the patient
options.B: They are hidden beneath heavy wool blankets
options.C: They rest securely on the foot of the bed
options.D: They hang freely without touching the floor

explanation: Always check those weights! If they touch the floor, they lose their pulling power and the therapy won't work. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h4)

question: You walk into a ward and see that your patient's traction weights are resting on the floor. What is your very next move?

options.A: Lift the weights and ensure they hang freely
options.C: Add more weight to make up for lost time
options.D: Document that the therapy is finished

explanation: Quick thinking! Just lift them up so they hang free again, and traction is instantly restored. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h4)

question: Why are frequent neurovascular checks so important for a patient in cervical traction?

options.A: To check if the patient is sleeping enough hours
options.B: To detect early signs of spinal cord or nerve compression
options.C: To prevent the skin from turning yellow
options.D: To measure how much water the patient is drinking

explanation: You want to catch any nerve trouble early! Checking movement and feeling in the arms and hands keeps the patient safe from permanent injury. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h5)

question: During an upper limb check, which finding means you need to report to the doctor right away?

options.C: Strong grip strength in both hands
options.D: New numbness or tingling in the fingers

explanation: Numbness and tingling are red flags! They tell you a nerve might be pinched or irritated and needs urgent attention. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h5)

question: What type of cleaning technique should a nurse use for skeletal traction pin sites?
explanation: Because those pins go straight into the bone, keeping things sterile is a must to stop germs from causing a bone infection. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h6)

question: Which sign around a skull pin site should ring alarm bells and be reported immediately?

options.A: A small amount of clear dried crusting
options.B: Mild redness that disappears within a day
options.C: Purulent yellow drainage and a foul odor
options.D: Normal skin color around the metal screw

explanation: Pus and bad smells always point to an infection setting in. Let the doctor know right away so it can be treated! [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h6)

question: A skull pin accidentally slips out while a patient is in traction. What is your very first emergency action?

options.A: Run out of the room to find the primary doctor
options.B: Remove the remaining pins with a bedside wrench
options.C: Add more weights to the traction rope system
options.D: Manually support the head in a neutral position

explanation: Don't panic! Hold the patient's head steady with your hands first to keep the neck safe, then call for help. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h7)

question: Which sudden problem can happen if the vagus nerve gets accidentally stimulated during traction setup?
explanation: The vagus nerve is powerful! Triggering it can cause the heart rate to slow right down and make the patient feel faint. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h7)
